q.t: What is a chord?
o: Three or more different notes played together
Two notes played one after another
A note held for a long time
q.e: A chord is several different notes sounding at once. Three notes = a triad.

q.t: A triad has how many different notes?
q.e: Tri = three.

q.t: A power chord is made of…
o: three notes a half step apart
q.e: Root + 5th — no 3rd. Written with a 5, like G5.

q.t: How is a power chord written?
q.e: The 5 stands for the 5th — the only note added to the root.

q.t: In a major or minor chord, which note decides the mood?
q.e: Major 3rd → bright; minor 3rd → sad. The root and 5th are the same in both.

q.t: What does Am mean?
q.e: Small m = minor.

q.t: What does a chord name with just a letter, like G, mean?
q.e: A letter on its own means a major chord.

q.t: What are the notes of C major?
q.e: Steps 1, 3, 5 of the C major scale.

q.t: Which chords are used most in rock with distortion?
q.e: Power chords stay clear under distortion because of the simple 3 : 2 ratio.

q.t: Em is played on six strings. How many different notes does it have?
q.e: E, G and B — the others are the same notes in other octaves.

q.t: A major triad stacks which half steps?
q.e: Root → major 3rd (4) → 5th (3 more) = 7.

q.t: A minor triad stacks which half steps?
q.e: Root → minor 3rd (3) → 5th (4 more) = 7.

q.t: What are the notes of A minor?
What are the notes of A major?
What are the notes of G major?
What are the notes of E minor?
E and Em differ only on the G string. Why?
o: That string is out of tune
The G string is the loudest
q.e: G (minor 3rd) vs G♯ (major 3rd) — the 3rd is the one note that changes.

q.t: Which shape plays a power chord with the root on the low E string?
o: A string, 2 frets higher than the root
Same fret on the A string
q.e: The perfect-5th shape: next string up, 2 frets higher.

q.t: Why is a power chord called 'neither major nor minor'?
o: It is too loud to tell
q.e: The 3rd decides major or minor — a power chord leaves it out.

q.t: Cm and CM mean…
q.e: Small m = minor; capital M = major. Read carefully!

q.t: What are the notes of D major?
What are the notes of D minor?
What are the notes of F major?
What are the notes of E major?
Which power chord has its root at fret 3 of the low E string?
q.e: Low E fret 3 = G, so G5 (G + D).

q.t: Which power chord has its root at fret 5 of the low E string?
q.e: Low E fret 5 = A, so A5 (A + E).

q.t: What two notes make G5?
q.e: Root G + perfect 5th (7 half steps up) = D.

q.t: Why does a power chord stay clear under distortion?
o: Its 3 : 2 ratio keeps the overtones lined up
It is quieter than other chords
q.e: Distortion adds many overtones; with a simple ratio they still line up, so no mud.

q.t: Why does a major chord tend to sound bright?
o: Its major 3rd matches the root's own overtones
q.e: One strong overtone of every note is a major 3rd above — a major chord agrees with it. (Habit plays a part too.)

q.t: Why do guitar chords repeat some notes?
o: Doubling makes the chord fuller, not different
To make it a different chord
q.e: Repeating notes in other octaves adds weight — the chord name depends only on the set of note names.

q.t: What are the notes of B minor?
What are the notes of C minor?
What are the notes of B major?
Which chord is A C E?
q.e: Root A, A → C = 3 (minor 3rd), A → E = 7. A minor.

q.t: Which chord is D F♯ A?
q.e: Root D, D → F♯ = 4 (major 3rd), D → A = 7. D major.

q.t: Which chord is G B♭ D?
q.e: G → B♭ = 3 (minor 3rd), G → D = 7. G minor.

q.t: You change C E G into C E♭ G. What has happened?
q.e: Lowering the 3rd by a half step turns major into minor.

q.t: A power chord with the root on the A string at fret 3 is…
q.e: A string fret 3 = C. So C5 (C + G).

q.t: In the open D chord (x x 0 2 3 2), which string carries the 3rd (F♯)?
q.e: D string = D, G string fret 2 = A, B string fret 3 = D, high e fret 2 = F♯.

q.t: Using steps 1-3-5 of the D major scale (D E F♯ G A B C♯), the D chord is…
q.e: Steps 1, 3, 5 = D, F♯, A.
